meta.title: Stepwise runs — one step, one run, one verdict
meta.description: The plan becomes the execution unit: each step gets its own generated prompt and its own run, verified against that step's own criteria before the next starts. A step that needs earlier work reopens it as rev_n and resumes. The mechanism lives in the CORE and both surfaces drive it — the native strip simply, the RFX planner with every control exposed.

frames.label: 2 · Drive — the new part: who decides what runs next
3 · Run — one step, start to verdict

nodes.label: The user's prompt
nodes.note: TODAY this same text is injected into every iteration of one long run, so the model must hold the whole task in mind at once and is trusted to touch each point on its own. In the new design it is used ONCE, to plan.

nodes.label: Step criteria
nodes.sublabel: each step declares a check that CAN FAIL · enforced at commit
nodes.note:
commit_plan gains a `verify` field per step: the concrete observation that proves the step done. Without it there is nothing to verify against and "done" falls back to guessing from disk — the bug in run-dataflow.

The model writes its own exam, so the SHAPE is constrained rather than the wording trusted (decided 2026-09-04). A verify must be one of three runnable forms:
  • a check_page eval that returns a boolean
  • a command whose exit code decides it
  • a file that must contain a named symbol

Existence-only checks are REJECTED at commit time, the way the plan gate already rejects a prose plan — "index.html exists" is the disk guess wearing a costume.

And a criterion can be impossible as easily as it can be lazy: the car run's own eval could never pass under file:// however correct the page was. So a step whose verify never passes gets a small budget, then hands back with the evidence. An unpassable check costs one step, never the task.

flags.title: Nothing has yet confirmed the model can write a usable verify
flags.note:
The whole design rests on the model declaring a check that is neither trivial nor impossible. commit_plan rejects the trivial ones, and a step whose check never passes hands back after two attempts rather than eating the task. Both are tested.

But every test so far uses a stub model. The real Qwen3.8-27B has never been asked for a verify, and it does not reliably call commit_plan as a tool at all — every run on record wrote its plan as prose, which the salvage path translates. Prose plans carry no verify, so they take the "no check declared" fallback and the run is unverified exactly as before.

So the machinery is proven and the input is not.
flags.fix: Run the fan or car prompt against the real Core and read the committed plan: does it carry verifies, are they runnable, do they pass when the step is genuinely done? If prose plans stay the norm, the salvage path needs to ask for checks too — or the plan gate needs to insist harder on the tool call.

nodes.label: Step supervisor
nodes.sublabel: owns the cursor: which step, which revision, what next
nodes.note:
The piece that does not exist today. It holds the step cursor, starts one run per step, reads each verdict and decides: advance, retry this step, or reopen an earlier one. It never writes code itself — it only decides what the next run is asked to do.

It is also the natural home for the turn budget: a stall or a loop ends THIS step's run, not the whole task, so the other steps still get their chance.

nodes.label: Step prompt writer
nodes.sublabel: the prompt for ONE step, carrying its check verbatim
nodes.note:
Assembled from committed facts rather than generated prose, so the prompt cannot drift from the plan it claims to execute. It carries the step, its files, its check quoted verbatim, and — as context — only the steps already VERIFIED. A failed step never appears as ground truth.

The user's original prompt is used once, to plan, and never re-injected. Re-injecting it into every iteration is what let one run wander across the whole task.

nodes.label: Revision decider
nodes.sublabel: reopen an earlier step as rev_n · cap 2 · re-verify downstream
nodes.note:
When a run reports that an EARLIER step is wrong or incomplete, the supervisor opens a revision run for that step — rev_2, rev_3 — with the new context explaining what is needed and why. When it passes, the cursor returns to where it left off. The model asks for this via a `needs_step` field on the verdict; the harness does not guess.

TWO RULES stop it looping, decided 2026-09-04:

1. CAP. Two revisions per step. The third request hands back to the user with every verdict on record, rather than spending the task on one disputed file.

2. RE-VERIFY DOWNSTREAM. A revision can invalidate a later step that was verified against the old file. After any revision, re-run the verify of every later step that shares a file with the revised one. Cheap — it is the declared check, not a new run — and it catches the silent breakage. If the same PAIR of steps fails twice, that is a genuine disagreement about the design: hand back with both verdicts instead of trying a third time.

nodes.label: Step run
nodes.sublabel: one step · its own prompt · its own budget · runPlanFrom
nodes.note: The existing agent loop, scoped to one step. Autopilot and a single step share one path (runPlanFrom) on purpose: a step run by a button must obey exactly the same rules as a step run by autopilot, or the surfaces drift apart again.

nodes.label: Step verify
nodes.sublabel: run the step's own check · pass / fail, with evidence · fails CLOSED
nodes.note:
Runs what the step declared: the eval, the command, the file check. The verdict is an observation, not the model's opinion that it is finished.

Every kind fails CLOSED. A check that cannot run is exactly as unproven as one that failed, and treating "could not check" as success is how a plan goes green while nothing works — the car run's check_page returned "eval produced no result" and that now reads as a failure.

nodes.label: checkpoint event
nodes.sublabel: step N, rev R — verdict, the check, its evidence, and why
nodes.note:
Written when a run ends, per step and revision, carrying the step INDEX so a revision's checkpoint is distinguishable from the first attempt's and two steps with the same name do not share a verdict.

This is the event BuildReportAt always preferred and had never once received, which is why status used to be guessed from disk.

nodes.label: events.jsonl
nodes.sublabel: one log · plan, runs, checkpoints, revisions

nodes.label: GET /report + /state
nodes.sublabel: status now comes from checkpoints, not from disk

nodes.label: Native plan strip
nodes.sublabel: SIMPLE surface · steps, which is running, pass/fail · no knobs
nodes.note:
What a user gets with no RFX pack installed. Shows the plan the moment it commits, marks the running step, shows each verdict as it lands, and offers ONE action: continue after a hand-back.

Not yet moved onto the step API: it still renders /report, which now carries real per-step status from checkpoints but not the cursor (next, blocked, revision).

nodes.label: RFX Planner panel
nodes.sublabel: ADVANCED surface · calls runStep(), no longer writes prompts
nodes.note:
~/.crv/rfx/planner/ui/panel.html. Its step buttons now call rfx.runStep(i) — the core scopes the run, executes it, checks it and records the verdict. Re-running a passed step calls runStep(i, true), a revision, which is what it is: a human saw something the check did not.

Its scenario rules (auto-continue, pause on failure, run a selected subset in order) stay in the panel — those are genuinely UI policy, unlike prompt-writing.

Still wip: the pack lives in ~/.crv/rfx and is not versioned with the repo.

ports.shape: POST run-step {step, rev?} · POST auto {on} · GET plan-state

nodes.label: Step control API
nodes.sublabel: GET /plan · POST /plan/step — the one way to drive a plan
nodes.note:
GET  /api/sessions/{id}/plan       the plan + per-step status, next, blocked
POST /api/sessions/{id}/plan/step  run one step (step -1 = whichever is next)

One contract so the two surfaces cannot drift apart. The cursor is rebuilt from the event log on every call rather than held in memory: a panel button, a CLI call and a resumed session must all see the same state, and the log is the only thing all three share.

The RFX bridge exposes the same two as rfx.plan() and rfx.runStep().
